schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark the elevation of Haman above all the princes; Ellicott doubts the Agagite descent, since Haman's name is Persian and Amalek was destroyed (1 Sam. 15), noting a Greek addition that calls him a Macedonian.
Clarke takes Haman a descendant of Agag whom Saul spared, the root of his hatred of the Jews; Wesley calls him an Amalekite of the royal seed set next to the king.
Henry reads the promotion morally: Esther could not prevent an enemy's rise; the king made a proud, passionate, revengeful man his favourite, for 'princes' darlings are not always worthies.'
Gill dates 'after these things' more than four or five years past Esther's marriage and the plot's discovery (Aben Ezra).

debates.question: Was Haman literally an Amalekite, descended from Agag?

sides.position: Yes, a descendant of Agag of the royal Amalekite seed, the ground of his enmity to the Jews
Doubtful; his name is Persian and Amalek was destroyed, and one Greek addition calls him a Macedonian

schools.summary: Clarke distinguishes the civil bow (kara), which the law allowed, from the divine prostration (shachah) Haman demanded, even by a statue; Wesley argues the express command proves a divine honour was meant, such as the Greeks refused the Persian kings.

Ellicott renders 'did not prostrate himself' and grounds the refusal in religious scruple; Keil notes prostration before a king was familiar among Israelites, so the objection lay in the Persian notions bound up with it.
Henry reads the refusal as conscience: religion forbade idolatrous honours to a wicked mortal and forbade flattering an Amalekite of the devoted nation (Ps. 15:4).
Gill notes the 'servants in the gate' were courtiers, not doorkeepers.

outliers.note: Grants the objection was mainly religious, but adds that whether Mordecai also recoiled from the ignominious character of the obeisance cannot be determined.

schools.summary: Keil reads the daily interrogation and the report 'to see whether his words would stand'; Mordecai's refusal rests on conscience, since prostration was familiar to Israelites and the objection lay only in the divine homage the Persians read into it.
Henry shows the courtiers pressing him daily with the command and the danger; his neighbours misread his steadfastness as pride, envy, or affectation, never as worship.
Gill pictures the servants watching Mordecai's carriage toward Haman from day to day before they challenge him.

themes: why transgressest thou the king's commandment

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects 'matters' to 'words' — whether Mordecai's plea that he might pay such reverence to God alone would hold good; Keil marks that the report drew Haman's eye to the man who would not bow.
Wesley reads 'to see' what the event would be, and takes 'for he was a Jew' as clearing Mordecai of pride: he refused from conscience, not arrogance.
Henry commends the steady, resolute conscience that would not conform though pressed daily, the confession that fixes the quarrel on a Jew's faith.
Gill notes the courtiers pressing him daily for his reasons and warning him of his danger before they told Haman.

Henry contrasts the meek man who would slight the affront with Haman's pride, which rages and boils over one unbent knee though it had a whole empire's adoration, and resolves at once that Mordecai must die.
Keil notes Haman saw for himself, as he next went in to the king, that Mordecai did not fall down, and was full of wrath.
Gill notes that after the informers spoke Haman watched Mordecai narrowly to see whether he would bow.

themes: the pride that cannot bear one slight
the resolve that Mordecai must die

schools.summary: Keil: in his pride Haman scorned to punish Mordecai alone; being shown 'the people of Mordecai,' he sought to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom.

Wesley traces the leap to implacable Amalekite hatred, fresh rage at Mordecai, and the judgment that every Jew shared his reason; the decree would reach even the returned Jews of the province of Judea.

Henry sees the ancient antipathy return: Saul son of Kish spared Agag, but Mordecai son of Kish (ch. 2:5) finds no mercy from this Agagite; Haman's wish is that of Ps. 83:4 to cut Israel off from being a nation.
Gill: Haman thought Mordecai too mean a satisfaction; nothing short of his whole people would content his vengeance.

themes: the whole nation marked for death
Saul and Agag reversed in Mordecai and Haman

schools.summary: Keil explains the recourse to the lot to fix a propitious day, the caster left unnamed as some astrologer; Ellicott notes the lot fell on the twelfth month, leaving nearly a year, and recalls Nisan as the Passover month.

Clarke supplies from the Greek that the lot chose the month Adar and a day within it; Wesley reads a settled malice overruled by God's singular providence, which disposed the lot to give the Jews room to escape.

Henry presses the irony: Haman's own superstition threw the day eleven months off, so the lot he trusted condemned him — God's wisdom serving its purposes by men's folly, a particular providence over the church.
Gill fixes Nisan as the first month of the sacred year and infers from the exact calendar that a Jew, likely Mordecai, wrote the book.

Keil calls the address subtly calculated; Ellicott exposes the charge of disloyalty as the persecutor's classic weapon (Ezra 4:13) and notes only a part of the nation had returned (42,360, Ezra 2:64), the rest scattered as Haman said.
Henry anatomizes the two-edged slander: the Jews painted as despicable (nameless vagabonds) and as dangerous (lawless, seditious) — enemies must first give a bad name to those they would destroy.
Clarke fastens on the grain of truth: their laws were diverse because they worshipped the true God by his own commandments, the very thing that made them precious turned into their crime.
Gill reads 'had said' and reasons Haman sought the king's leave before casting lots for the day.

themes: a lie wrapped around a truth
a people set apart, painted as set against the king

schools.summary: Keil gives the full terms of the proposal; Ellicott sets ten thousand talents at near two and a half millions, more than two-thirds of the empire's yearly revenue, to be met from Haman's wealth or the victims' plunder.
Clarke marks the cunning of asking it be 'written' into law, throwing the odium onto the king, and defends the plausibility of so vast a sum from Herodotus and Plutarch.
Henry: the bribe answers the king's one objection about lost revenue, but Haman meant to reimburse himself from the spoil (v.13), making the victims pay for their own ruin.
Gill reads the plain request for a law signed and sealed and letters sent everywhere to order the destruction.

themes: the bribe as mask and lure

schools.summary: Keil weighs the signet as giving the edict, drafted in the king's name, the authority of an irrevocable decree, and marks the pointed epithet 'the Jews' enemy.'
Gill: the ring was the Persian bond of highest friendship, given to seal the letters; Esther cannot yet have told the king her people, or he would not have armed their enemy.
Clarke explains the ring carried the privy seal, worn on the finger, that would give Haman's writing full force among the provincial governors.
Henry indicts the heedless king who gave up a people as lambs to the lion — a kingdom miserable at the disposal of a head with one ear and a nose to be led by.

Keil reads 'the silver is given to thee' as a screen against the appearance of a bribe; Ellicott finds the reply incredible yet true to Xerxes, an indolent king handing over a whole nation and its goods.
Henry: the king will not even say 'kill them,' but gives Haman people and silver alike, abandoning a whole nation to private malice with a shrug, never asking if the charge were true.
Gill takes the words to mean the king out of munificence refused the ten thousand talents and returned them.

debates.question: Does 'the silver is given to thee' mean the king refused the bribe or bestowed it on Haman?

sides.position: He genuinely declined the money, returning it out of munificence
A face-saving formality: he awards the silver to Haman lest he seem bribed, handing over people and possessions alike

themes: the silver is given to thee
a nation handed over with a shrug

schools.summary: Keil spreads out the apparatus — satraps, governors, rulers of every people, each in its own script and tongue, sealed with the king's ring; Ellicott traces 'lieutenants' to the Persian original behind 'satrap' and recalls, with Wordsworth, that the thirteenth of Nisan was the eve of Passover.
Clarke notes 'the king's lieutenants' renders a Persian word, the satraps, only transliterated in the Hebrew.
Gill dates the summoning of the king's scribes to the thirteenth of Nisan, to write the letters.

themes: satraps and every province and tongue

schools.summary: Keil confirms the Persian post-riders from Herodotus and gives the threefold sentence — destroy, kill, cause to perish all Jews of every age and both sexes in one day — with the spoil named to whet greed; Ellicott glosses 'posts' as the royal runners.
Clarke sees a general massacre in which whoever killed a Jew took his property, arming every man's covetousness, and recalls the fuller decree preserved in the Greek and Latin.
Gill describes the swift mounted couriers (angari) whom neither snow nor rain nor heat nor darkness could stay.

themes: destroy, kill, and cause to perish

schools.summary: Keil fixes the notice that the copy sent into every province was 'galui' — opened, unsealed — so a law might be given openly to all peoples, that they be ready; Ellicott glosses the Persian 'pathshegen' ('copy'), found only here and twice more in the book.
Gill: besides the sealed letters, a summary was proclaimed by heralds and posted openly, that the common people everywhere might be ready.

Keil completes the scene — couriers hastened, the decree promulgated at Susa, the king and Haman at their cups while the city is 'perplexed' (as Joel 1:18); Ellicott hears in the city's dismay its sympathy with the Jews and against Haman.

Clarke enlarges on the danger to the whole city once the mob was armed, denouncing the measure and despotism itself; Wesley reads the citizens' grief as kinship, common dealing, and humanity toward innocents appointed like sheep for slaughter.

Henry draws the closing contrast of merry court and sad city: Haman keeps the king drinking lest conscience wake — the cursed method of drowning convictions — while it is impious to feast when the church is in distress.
Gill notes the posts went out hastened by the king's command, to make all speed.

outliers.note: Turns the verse into a denunciation of despotic government as the standing curse of a nation — the king an idiot, his counsellors madmen — beyond what the other witnesses draw from it.

themes: the court's feast and the city's dread
